description: Use case: the Swiss vote of 28 February 2027 on lifting the ban on new nuclear power plants (amendment of the Nuclear Energy Act, indirect counter-proposal to the initiative 'Jederzeit Strom für alle (Blackout stoppen)', referendum filed with 131793 signatures). The file holds the numbers of the main studies of both sides (ETH/PSI white paper of June 2026, BAK Economics for economiesuisse of July 2026, Swiss Academies of August 2026, SES, Fraunhofer ISE, operator cost, ElCom tariffs), the pro and contra claims as supports and limits triples on the phrase 'lifting the NPP ban', and the formulas of a decision calculator: from the overnight construction cost, the cost of capital, the construction time and the capacity the levelised cost of the new plant, against the cost of the renewable alternative plus the shifted winter trade and an optional security value; the annual cost difference spread over the demand of 2050 is the average cost difference in Rp per kWh, and its ratio to a threshold gives the verdict yes, no or undecided. The BAK base case is reproduced in the calc-validation chain (12.137 TWh, 17264 million CHF, 114.4 CHF per MWh, 612 million CHF subsidy, average cost difference -0.009 Rp per kWh: undecided). The html prototype npp_ch_vote_sample.html renders this use case stand-alone. The sliders, presets, tags, arguments, verdict, difference column, cells and sensitivity table of the page are the proposed elements of docs/json_structure.md. Values without a source are the calculator defaults and are tagged assumed with their own confidence; the measured values carry their study as source. Not in the file: the Academies report pdf itself (numbers via sda), the Axpo Energy Report 2026 and Schwarz et al. 2023 (both only via BAK), the VSE demand projection of 90 TWh, a CO2 price, risk costs and the grid expansion difference between central and decentral supply.

triples.name: supply gap supports lifting the NPP ban
triples.description: The four existing plants deliver {num:36 %} of Swiss electricity and almost half of the winter electricity; the last one (Leibstadt) is expected to stop around 2044, while demand rises to about {num:76 TWh} by 2050. Without new plants the winter net import grows to {num:7.5 TWh} in 2050; one EPR cuts it to {num:3.2 TWh}. {source:BAK economiesuisse study 2026}

triples.name: competitiveness supports lifting the NPP ban
triples.description: With state support and financing at {num:5 %} instead of 8 %, two of four ETH/PSI models build {num:2 GW} at {num:8'000 CHF/kW}, and all four build {num:2.6 to 4.9 GW} at 5'000 CHF/kW. {source:ETH PSI white paper 2026}

triples.name: price stability supports lifting the NPP ban
triples.description: A new plant lowers the average wholesale price by {num:7 to 9 CHF/MWh} and dampens winter peaks of {num:130 to 135 CHF/MWh}; the avoided price volatility, outage and shortage risks are valued at about {num:520 million CHF} per year. {source:BAK economiesuisse study 2026}

triples.name: value added supports lifting the NPP ban
triples.description: About {num:1.6 billion CHF} value added and {num:2'900 full-time jobs} per year over 60 years of operation (study commissioned by economiesuisse). {source:BAK economiesuisse study 2026}

triples.name: option supports lifting the NPP ban
triples.description: Lifting the ban keeps the nuclear option open; whether a plant is built is decided later on cost and demand. {source:ETH PSI white paper 2026}{source:Swiss Academies NPP cost report 2026}

triples.name: subsidy need limits lifting the NPP ban
triples.description: Even the pro study calculates a levelised cost of {num:115.5 CHF/MWh} against a market price of {num:64 CHF/MWh}: the market pays 55 %, the state about {num:625 million CHF} per year. No Western new build of the last twenty years was financed without state support. {source:BAK economiesuisse study 2026}

triples.name: cost overrun limits lifting the NPP ban
triples.description: The Swiss Academies of Sciences put the cost of one plant at {num:14 billion CHF} (Westinghouse AP1000) or {num:21 billion CHF} (EDF EPR) in the optimistic case, {num:25} or {num:43 billion CHF} if the overruns of Olkiluoto, Flamanville, Hinkley Point and Vogtle repeat. {source:Swiss Academies NPP cost report 2026}

triples.name: timing limits lifting the NPP ban
triples.description: About {num:23 years} from the vote to commercial operation (2050); the existing plants stop in the 2030s and 2040s. The head of the largest nuclear operator fears ten years of debate with nothing built. {source:BAK economiesuisse study 2026}{source:SRF Axpo energy report 2026}

triples.name: net zero
triples.description: the Swiss climate target of net zero greenhouse-gas emissions by 2050

triples.name: net zero limits lifting the NPP ban
triples.description: All four models reach net zero 2050 with {num:36 to 43 TWh} of solar and {num:0.3 to 8.6 TWh} of wind; hydro and PV form three quarters of the supply. Winter imports stay in every scenario, with or without new plants. {source:ETH PSI white paper 2026}

triples.name: cluster risk limits lifting the NPP ban
triples.description: A residual risk and a single large unit (1.6 GW, about 16 % of demand) whose outage must be covered - the pro study leaves the risk side out; an insurance study prices the risk below 0.0001 Rp/kWh, the opponents call it uninsurable. {source:BAK economiesuisse study 2026}{source:SSES position paper 2025}
the subsidy need is the number both sides read differently: a cost of state support for the no side, the price of secured winter supply for the yes side

triples.name: new NPP more
triples.description: The Swiss electorate decides whether the ban on building new nuclear power plants (NPP), in force since 2018, is lifted again. Parliament passed the amendment of the Nuclear Energy Act as the indirect counter-proposal to the "Blackout stoppen" initiative; the referendum against it was filed with about 132'000 signatures in October 2026 {source:SRF Blackout initiative 2026}{source:20 Minuten referendum filed 2026}. A yes only allows new plants; the build decision would follow in the 2030s and a plant would run from about 2050 {source:ETH PSI white paper 2026}{source:BAK economiesuisse study 2026}. Below are the arguments of both sides with their numbers, then a calculator: set your own assumptions with the sliders and see whether a new plant, under these assumptions, lowers or raises the average electricity cost in 2050 - and what that suggests for your vote.

triples.name: new NPP detail tables label
triples.description: Formulas and sources

triples.name: new NPP note model limits
triples.description: annual balance in prices of 2024 for one year of operation around 2050, no hourly dispatch, no learning or escalation of costs over time, no construction delay beyond the construction time set, no risk cost, no CO₂ price, no grid expansion difference between central and decentral supply; the ETH/PSI models and the BAK balance model are the places to look for these effects

formulas.name: annual production formula
formulas.description: the electricity of the plant in TWh: the capacity in GW times the capacity factor times the hours of a year; GW times hours gives GWh, divided by 1000 TWh

formulas.name: interest during construction formula
formulas.expression: "interest during construction" = "overnight construction cost" * "capacity" * "WACC" * "construction time" * "interest-during-construction factor"
formulas.latex: IDC = OCC \cdot P \cdot r \cdot T_{build} \cdot f_{IDC}
formulas.description: the interest on the capital spent before operation in million CHF: CHF per kW times GW is million CHF; the factor is the share of the construction time over which the capital is on average outstanding

formulas.name: investment formula
formulas.description: the total capital until commercial operation in million CHF

formulas.name: annuity factor formula
formulas.description: the share of the investment to recover every year

formulas.name: capital cost formula
formulas.description: the annual recovery of the investment per MWh: million CHF per TWh equals CHF per MWh

formulas.name: levelised cost formula
formulas.description: capital cost plus operating cost per MWh

formulas.name: subsidy need formula
formulas.description: what the market does not pay, in million CHF per year; zero if the levelised cost is below the market price

formulas.name: alternative cost formula
formulas.description: the levelised cost of the renewable alternative plus the system cost of intermittent supply per MWh

formulas.name: shifted energy formula
formulas.description: the energy the new NPP moves from winter imports to summer exports: its production times the difference of its winter share and the winter share of the renewable alternative

formulas.name: trade value formula
formulas.description: the value of the shifted trade in million CHF per year: avoided winter imports minus lost summer exports

formulas.name: winter net import formula
formulas.expression: "winter net import with new NPP" = "winter net import" - "shifted energy"
formulas.description: the winter net import with the new NPP: the winter net import without it minus the shifted energy

formulas.name: security value formula
formulas.description: the value of the secured winter supply in million CHF per year: the shifted energy times the value per MWh the reader sets

formulas.name: cost difference formula
formulas.expression: "cost difference" = "annual production" * "levelised cost" - "annual production" * "alternative cost" - "trade value" - "annual security value"
formulas.latex: \Delta C = E \cdot LCOE - E \cdot c_{alt} - V_{trade} - V_{sec}
formulas.description: the annual cost with the new NPP minus the annual cost without it in million CHF; negative means the new NPP is cheaper

formulas.name: average cost formula
formulas.description: the cost difference spread over all consumption in Rp per kWh: million CHF per TWh is 0.1 Rp per kWh

formulas.name: household price formula
formulas.description: the household price in the scenario with the new NPP: the energy tariff without it plus the average cost difference plus grid, metering and levies; the levies value carries the grid part too

formulas.name: household bill formula
formulas.description: the annual bill of an H4 household in CHF

formulas.name: break-even construction cost formula
formulas.expression: "break-even construction cost" = ("alternative cost" + ("winter share" - "renewable winter share") * ("import price" - "export price" + "security value") - "operating cost") / ("annuity factor" * (1 + "WACC" * "construction time" * "interest-during-construction factor") / ("capacity factor" * 8760) * 1000)
formulas.latex: OCC^{*} = \frac{c_{alt} + (ws_{NPP} - ws_{ren})(p_{imp} - p_{exp} + v_{sec}) - c_{op}}{a (1 + r T_{build} f_{IDC}) \cdot 1000 / (CF \cdot 8760)}
formulas.description: the overnight construction cost at which both options cost the same: the levelised cost that makes the cost difference zero minus the operating cost, divided by the capital cost per MWh of one CHF per kW

formulas.name: verdict formula
formulas.description: a ratio below -1 is yes (new NPP cheaper by more than the threshold), above +1 is no, in between undecided; the verdict of the page compares the average cost with the threshold

formulas.name: investment in billion formula
formulas.description: the investment of the result table in billion CHF

formulas.name: annual cost with new NPP formula
formulas.expression: "annual cost with new NPP" = "annual production" * "levelised cost"
formulas.description: the annual cost of the compared kilowatt-hours with the new plant

formulas.name: annual cost without new NPP formula
formulas.expression: "annual cost without new NPP" = "annual production" * "alternative cost" + "trade value" + "annual security value"
formulas.description: the annual cost of the same kilowatt-hours from the renewable alternative plus the value of the shifted trade and the secured supply

formulas.name: energy cost with new NPP formula
formulas.expression: "energy cost with new NPP" = "energy tariff" + "average cost"
formulas.description: the energy tariff with the new plant is the tariff without it plus the average cost difference

formulas.name: household price without new NPP formula
formulas.description: the energy tariff plus grid, metering and levies without the new plant

formulas.name: household bill without new NPP formula
formulas.expression: "household bill without new NPP" = "household price without new NPP" * 4500 / 100
formulas.description: the price times 4'500 kWh without the new plant

formulas.name: average cost change formula
formulas.description: the size of the average cost difference for the text of the verdict

formulas.name: household bill change formula
formulas.expression: "household bill change" = abs( "household bill" - "household bill without new NPP" )
formulas.description: the size of the difference of the household bill for the text of the verdict

sources.name: ETH PSI white paper 2026
sources.description: Bardow A, Burgherr P, Darudi A, Fernandez de Losada L, Filippini M, Guidati G, Hug G, Lordan-Perret R, Manera A, McKenna R, Moret S, Panos E, Patt A, Pautz A, Sansavini G, Schaffner C, Schmidt T, Savelsberg J, Turan E (2026). Nuclear Power and the Future Swiss Energy System: A Techno-Economic Modelling Analysis. Joint White Paper by ETH Zurich and the Paul Scherrer Institute, 29 June 2026. Four energy system models, 45 TWh expansion target, net zero 2050. Numbers taken from the PSI media release of the same day.

sources.name: BAK economiesuisse study 2026
sources.description: BAK Economics (2026). Volkswirtschaftliche Auswirkungen eines Ersatzneubaus der Schweizer Kernkraftwerke. Study commissioned by economiesuisse, July 2026. Base case: one EPR of 1.63 GW, commercial operation 2050, 60 years, capacity factor 85 percent, WACC 5 percent after tax, prices of 2024. Commissioned by the business federation that campaigns for a yes; the LCOE inputs come from Schwarz et al. 2023 (ETH Nexus-e) and the Axpo Energy Report 2026.
